overview.body:
**Shikoku** ​(*shikoku*) ‌— Smallest ‌Main ​Island ​— belongs ​to ​the ​Japanese tradition. ‌The ​name ​means "Four ‌provinces"[^1].

​Shikoku ‌is ​the smallest ‌of ​Japan's ​four main ​islands ​and ​the setting ‌of ​the ‌great eighty-eight-temple ​Buddhist ‌pilgrimage.

​PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name ‌as ​**Shikoku**. The ​plain ‌ASCII ‌form *shikoku* ‌is ​the ​modern Hepburn ‌romanization; ​the ​restoration ‌capitalizes the ​conventional ​spelling. ‌Because the ​Japanese ‌source ​script uses ​logographic ​characters ​whose ‌distinctive visual ‌form ​cannot ‌be conveyed ​in ​the ‌basic Latin ‌alphabet, ‌and ‌because no ​diacritic ‌or ​special ​letter is ​added ‌in ​this restoration, ​the ​name ‌is placed ​in ​Tier ​2. The ‌Unicode ​form ‌remains ​the philologically ‌complete ​reference, ‌while the ‌ASCII ​spelling ​is a ​practical ​convenience ‌for the ‌domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**四国**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Four provinces"[^1].

​Shikoku means ​"four provinces," ‌from *shi* ​(four) and ​*koku* (province). ‌The name ​refers to ‌the four ​ancient provinces ‌of Iyo, ​Tosa, Sanuki, ​and Awa ​that comprised ​the island. ​It is ‌the smallest ​of Japan's ‌four main ​islands and ‌is most ​famous today ‌for the ​eighty-eight-temple Buddhist pilgrimage.

‌The ASCII ​form *shikoku* ​survives only ‌because the ‌early domain-name ‌system could ​not carry ​Japanese characters ‌or diacritics; ​it is ​a technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Shikoku** gives ‌the conventional ​Hepburn romanization ​with initial ​capitalization, the ​standard scholarly ‌way to ‌cite a ​proper name ‌in romanized ​Japanese. The ​name is ‌Tier 2 ‌because the ‌restoration does not ‌add a ​distinctive diacritic ‌or special ​letter absent ​from the ​ASCII form.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **s** ​→ **S** ‌— Same
​- **h** ​→ **h** ​— Same
‌- **i** ​→ **i** ‌— Same
​- **k** ‌→ **k** ​— Same
‌- **o** ‌→ **o** ​— Same
​- **k** ​→ **k** ​— Same
‌- **u** ‌→ **u** ​— Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/ɕi.ko.kɯ/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'SHIKOKU' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Shikoku ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*shikoku* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Shikoku** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Shikoku** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*shikoku* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Shikoku ​is the ‌domain ‌of pilgrimage, ​ascetic practice, ​and ​rural sacred ​landscape. ​The eighty-eight ‌temples associated ​with ​Kūkai (Kōbō ‌Daishi) ​make it ‌one of ​the ‌world's great ​pilgrimage ​circuits. The ​island also ​preserves ​ancient Shinto ‌shrines, ​*kabuki* traditions, ‌and ​a distinctive ‌dialect and ​food ‌culture.

The ​domain ‌of **Shikoku** ​is understood ​within ‌the broader ‌Japanese ‌religious landscape ​as both ​a ‌specific functional ​sphere ​and a ‌node in ​a ​network of ‌kami, ​buddhas, and ‌local ​spirits. Shrines, ​temples, and ​household ​rites all ‌invoke ‌the figure ​in ways ‌that ​blur strict ​boundaries ‌between Shinto ‌and Buddhist ‌practice[^3]. ‌The restoration ​**Shikoku** ‌therefore names ​not only ​a ​mythic person ‌but ​a living ​field ​of ritual ‌activity: pilgrimage, ​festival, ​iconography, and ​prayer ‌continue to ​define what ‌the ​name means ‌in ​contemporary Japan. ‌This combinatory ‌or ​"syncretic" context ​is ​essential for ​interpreting the ‌domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
The ​mythology of ‌Shikoku is ‌inseparable ​from the ​life of ​Kūkai (774–835), ​the ​founder of ‌Shingon Buddhism. ​Tradition ​holds that ‌he established ​the eighty-eight ‌temples, ​and pilgrims ‌today believe ​that ​he walks ​with them ​in ​spirit. The ‌island's mountains, ​capes, and ‌springs ​are dotted ‌with sites ​where ‌Kūkai is ​said to ‌have ​practised austerities ​or performed ‌miracles.

The ‌narrative ‌of **Shikoku** ​participates in ​the ‌larger mythic ​program of ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ​*Nihon Shoki*: ​to explain ‌the ​origins of ‌the imperial ​house, ​the division ​of divine ​labour, and ‌the ‌relationship between ​the human ‌and ​kami worlds. ​Because these ‌chronicles were ‌compiled ‌in the ‌eighth century ​under ‌imperial patronage, ​the myths ​also ​serve a ‌political theology, ​grounding earthly ​authority ​in divine ‌descent and ​cosmic ​order[^3]. Read ​comparatively, the ‌story ​of shikoku ‌illustrates how ​Japanese myth ‌uses ​genealogy, descent ‌from heaven, ‌and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains to ​construct ‌a coherent ‌sacred history.
​

sources.citation: Kūkai and Shingon Buddhism: tradition of the eighty-eight temples.
Shinto: The Kami Way, Ono Sokyo, 1962.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon ‌Shoki* do ​not treat ​**Shikoku** ​primarily as ​a ​mythic person ‌but ​as a ​place embedded ‌in ​the sacred ‌geography ​of the ‌Japanese ​archipelago. The ​chronicles map ​the ​land by ​assigning ‌divine origins ​to ‌its mountains, ​rivers, ‌plains, and ​islands, so ‌a ​site such ‌as ​Shikoku participates ​in ‌this cosmogonic ‌project even ‌when ​it is ​not ‌the protagonist ​of ​a single ‌episode[^1]. Later ​records, ​including the ‌provincial ​*fudoki*, elaborate ‌the ​local kami ​and traditions ​that ​grew up ‌around ‌the place.

​For ‌scholars, the ​value of ​the ‌*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon ‌Shoki* lies ‌in ​their preservation ‌of an ​eighth-century ​vision of ​the ‌land as ​a ​realm charged ​with ‌kami presence. ​Shikoku appears ​within ​that vision ‌as ​the island ‌of ​the eighty-eight-temple ‌Buddhist pilgrimage ​and ‌regional Shinto ‌cults, ​a status ​that ​shaped pilgrimage, ​poetry, and ‌political ‌rhetoric for ​centuries[^2].

shinto-sources.body:
The ​Shinto ‌sources for ‌**Shikoku** ​centre ​on ​shrine ​records, ritual ​protocols, ‌and ​the ​priestly ‌traditions that ​maintain ‌the ​site's ‌cult. Shrine ​chronicles ​(*engi*) ​compiled ​from ​the medieval ‌period ​onward ‌recount ​the foundation, ‌miraculous ​origins, ‌and ​patronage ‌of Shikoku, ​while ​liturgical ‌texts ‌preserve ‌the *norito* ​prayers ​offered ‌there[^1]. ​Archaeological and ​architectural ‌evidence ​complements ​these ‌written sources, ​showing ‌how ​the ​site's ​sacred topography ​was ‌developed ‌over ​centuries.

Because ‌Shikoku ​is ​a ‌place, ‌its Shinto ‌identity ‌is ​inseparable ‌from ​the landscape: ​trees, ​springs, ‌rocks, ​and pathways ​all ​function ‌as ​secondary ​scriptures. The ​ritual ‌calendar ​of ‌the shrine—festivals, ​pilgrimages, ‌and ​imperial ‌envoys—provides ‌the living ​context ​in ​which ​the ‌written sources ‌are ​activated[^2].

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
**Shikoku** ​bears ‌a significant ‌Buddhist ​imprint, ​whether ​through ​the presence ​of ‌temples, ​the ​pilgrimage ‌routes that ​traverse ‌the ​site, ‌or the ​medieval ​doctrine ​that ​local ​kami are ‌manifestations ​of ‌Buddhist ​buddhas and ‌bodhisattvas[^1]. ​The ‌*honji-suijaku* ​theory ‌provided the ​theological ​vocabulary ‌for ‌this ‌identification: the ​kami ​of ‌Shikoku ​could be ​understood ‌as ​a ​*suijaku*, ‌or local ​trace, ‌of ​a ​universal ​Buddhist principle.

​After ‌the ‌Meiji ​separation of ‌Shinto ​and ​Buddhism, ‌many ‌Buddhist structures ‌and ‌images ​were ‌removed ​from shrine ​precincts, ​yet ‌the ​artistic, architectural, ​and ​ritual ‌layers ​remain ​visible to ​historians[^2]. ‌Shikoku ​thus ‌preserves a ​palimpsest ‌of ​Japanese ‌religious ‌history, in ​which ​Buddhist ​and ​Shinto ‌claims have ‌alternately ​dominated.

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
